newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Deal reached on Mostar, international envoy says.
newsitem.headline: Deal reached on Mostar, international envoy says.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation and international officials reached an agreement on Wednesday to resolve the crisis in the divided south Bosnian town of Mostar, an international envoy said.

"We reached an agreement on Mostar that contains twelve very operative points," Michael Steiner, deputy to the International High Representative Carl Bildt, told reporters after the meeting in the Sarajevo presidency building.

In an attempt to defuse tensions, Croat and Moslem officials including Federation president Kresimir Zubak, a Croat, and Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, held a meeting behind closed doors.
General William Crouch, commander of the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) for Bosnia, Steiner and acting U.N. police commissioner Robert Wasserman also attended.
Both sides strongly condemned recent violence in Mostar and the evictions of Mostar citizens, Steiner said.
Croats opened fire on Moslem pilgrims trying to visit a cemetery in the Croat quarter on Monday. At least one was killed and 22 wounded.

The participants in the meeting reconfirmed a request to the United Nations International Police Task Force (IPTF) to conduct an independent investigation, Steiner said, adding that a report should identify those responsible for the escalation of violence and the attacks on Mostar citizens. It is expected to be completed within a week.
Steiner stressed the participants agreed they would accept and endorse the IPTF report and that perpetrators would be arrested and brought to trial.
"I will recommend to the European Union to bar individuals responsible for human rights violations... from travelling to the European Union," he told reporters.

Among other issues agreed were the immediate return of evicted people, the continuation of a curfew in Mostar until the situation allows its suspension, an increased SFOR presence to remain and telephone lines between the two parts of city to be reconnected, a statement issued after the meeting said.

"I think this is a good agreement, an operational agreement. It was important that the federation partners took up their responsibilities ... but the most important thing is that this agreement is also implemented," Steiner said.

Asked what made him believe the agreement would be respected this time after so many violations of agreements in the past, Steiner answered:"I think if people know they cannot travel any more to European Union countries, hopefully also to others, that is a new element."
